fixes.explanation: Psalm 9:3 says, "When my enemies retreat, they stumble and perish before You." Retreating doesn't get them out of it. The verse puts the retreat and the stumbling together. This is a heavy line, friend.
Psalm 9:9 says, "The LORD is a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble." Both of those are places you can run INTO. In times of trouble, that's what David says the LORD is, baker.
Try that word in the sentence, friend. Saying He does not hear the cry would be a different claim than the one David makes. Psalm 9:12 says, "He does not ignore the cry of the afflicted."
Good word, but it isn't the one in the line, friend. David doesn't use it here. Psalm 9:12 says, "He does not ignore the cry of the afflicted." The word that fits the blank is ignore.
Psalm 9:14 gives his purpose: "…that I may declare all Your praises…" He also wants to "…rejoice in Your salvation." Praise and rejoicing are what he's asking to be lifted up for, baker.

A quiet getaway sounds nice, friend, but that's not what he says. In Psalm 9:14 he asks to be lifted up so that he may "…declare all Your praises…" and "…rejoice in Your salvation." His wish is praise and rejoicing, not rest.
Psalm 9:20 says, "let the nations know they are but men." It's a humbling reminder, baker. That's the whole ask in this line.
Psalm 10:2 says, "In pride the wicked pursue the needy…" They do it in pride. The needy are the ones being pursued, baker.
The psalm doesn't mention kings here. It says, "In pride the wicked pursue the needy…" The ones being chased are the needy, baker.

That would at least leave a little room for Him, and the verse doesn't. It says, "In his pride the wicked man does not seek Him; in all his schemes there is no God." (Psalm 10:4) All his schemes means all of them.

The verse doesn't mention any special day. It says, "In his pride the wicked man does not seek Him; in all his schemes there is no God." (Psalm 10:4) No God in all his schemes means no room made for Him.
Right, baker. The first half is true. But Psalm 10:5 says, "Your lofty judgments are far from him…" They're far from him, not close.

Psalm 10:11 says, "He says to himself, “God has forgotten; He hides His face and never sees.”" That's what the wicked man tells himself, baker. It's his claim about God, and I'm glad the psalm doesn't leave it standing alone.
Forgiveness isn't in this verse, friend. In Psalm 10:11 he says to himself, “God has forgotten; He hides His face and never sees.” That's the line the psalm gives him.
He doesn't say that. Psalm 10:11 has him saying, “God has forgotten; He hides His face and never sees.” Nothing in his line claims God is fighting for him, baker.
Psalm 10:14 says, "The victim entrusts himself to You; You are the helper of the fatherless." The LORD is the helper of the fatherless, baker. That's a good thing to have in your corner.
The verse doesn't call Him the helper of the powerful, friend. It says, "You are the helper of the fatherless." (Psalm 10:14) The victim is the one who entrusts himself to the LORD.

Psalm 10:15 says, "Break the arm of the wicked and evildoer; call him to account for his wickedness until none is left to be found." That's the psalmist's request to God, baker. What he asks God to break is the arm.
